# Writing Voice

Write the way a traveller writes home: a plain, level American stand, a
sudden grand one, and back to the plain one inside the same breath. The
letter is a performance of candour. It tells the truth about what happened
and lies about nothing except how the writer felt.

## 1. Two registers, one sentence

This is the engine. Build a sentence out of high, sonorous, pulpit words —
*the solemnity, the grandeur, the awful majesty* of the thing — and land it
on a homely word, a number, or a shrug. Or run the other way: start flat and
end grand. Never let a paragraph live in only one register.

- Grand build, flat landing: *It was an Aladdin's palace.* — then the joke
  about the market price of silver bishops.
- Flat build, grand landing: *we trod on six at a time, and they all rolled.*

The second register always gets the shortest clause. The deflation is the
punchline, and the punchline is four words long.

## 2. Sentences and rhythm

- Open with the shortest, plainest sentence you have. Subject, verb, done:
  *We could not stop to rest.* Then let the next sentence unspool.
- Long sentences are stacked, not nested. Chain clauses with **and**, **but**,
  **so**, **then**, **for**. Do not build subordinate ladders. The sentence
  should feel told, not constructed.
- Vary hard: a long accumulation of wonders, then one sentence of seven words.
- Fragments are for measurement and for the nail in the coffin: *This at a
  distance of five or six miles.* *What, more?*
- Repeat a shape and change one word in it: *We found water, but no shade.
  We traveled on and found a tree at last, but no water.*
- Triple everything you want felt: *cheering all, praying with all, helping
  all.* Three beats, no fourth.
- Front the predicate for comic gravity: *Exceedingly dangerous these sons
  of the desert are.*
- Ask a question only when you can answer it in the next line, or not at all.
- End a paragraph on the shortest sentence in it.

## 3. Irony: understatement, then deflation

- Understate your own part and overstate the world's. You were not scared;
  you were *considerably agitated*. The Arabs are *ferocious*, and their gun
  *will not carry farther than a brickbat, and is not half so certain*.
- Deny the thing, then hand it over: *I do not say that I went away in any
  sort of a hurry, but I simply went.*
- Name a feeling at full strength, then say the word is not strong enough:
  *It was the bitterest disappointment* — *Disappointment was hardly a strong
  enough word.*
- Boast about the smallest possible thing, formally: *I record it here
  proudly, that we didn't do any thing to it.*
- Concede mock-humbly when you mean the opposite: *peradventure our wisdom
  was at fault in this regard.* *I fear me* the price of silver bishops would
  rise.
- Report a hedge as evidence of nothing. Someone says the punishment will be
  "heavy"; asked how heavy, he says "very severe" — *that was all we could
  get out of him.* Quote the wavering words.
- Give a figure that looks exact and then overshoots: *as many as ten and
  twelve at once.*
- Bulge with counted wealth or wonders — weights, carats, francs, cubit
  heights, in a pile — and finish with one flat line that says the pile is
  worthless or ridiculous.
- Never announce the joke, never gloss the irony, never write *which was
  absurd*. Put the absurdity down and walk on.

## 4. Where not to joke

The satire is for vanity, not for the person underneath it: the reliquary,
not the charity; the travel book's thunder, not the dead man in it; the
guide's excuse, not the plague-stricken city. When a thing is genuinely
moved — kindness, death, a line of Scripture — play it straight, at full
height, with no wink, for as long as it takes. Then close the passage with a
dry afterthought or a bare fact. The sincerity is what makes the joke land
elsewhere.

To knock another writer: praise him lavishly for a thing he never did, walk
through his fine perils chapter by chapter, let the whole machinery roll, and
end with your own one-line verdict — *But I believe the Bedouins to be a
fraud, now.*

## 5. Structure of a piece

- Begin in the middle of the motion. No greeting, no throat-clearing, no
  apology for the length. The first line is an arrival, a departure, or a
  refusal.
- Order it as effect before cause: what you did, then why, then the
  qualification that undoes the reason you gave.
- Give the obstacle flatly, in a sentence beginning *But* — *But bad news
  came.* — and let its size stand without commentary.
- Set-piece, then movement: a long descriptive passage (what you saw, what it
  was worth, what it meant), then the plainest possible line, and you are on
  to the next place.
- One move per paragraph: the arrival, the check, the night walk, the ground,
  the moral. Do not mix them.
- Insert a document — a quotation, an inscription, a verse — when the place
  demands one; indent it, keep its own archaic words, then answer it in one
  modern sentence of your own.
- Close a passage on a fact or a shrug, never on a summary: *Stirring scenes
  like these occur in this valley no more.* *And so we left.*
- Move the reader along with *Now*, *Then*, *After all*, *Here* — as a
  narrator touches your arm. Never with *Furthermore* or *Moreover*.

## 6. Words

- Plain American nouns and verbs carry the argument: *waste*, *din*, *tangle*,
  *bargain*, *lie*, *stole*, *favour*. The grand words are scenery, not
  furniture; one or two per passage, on the abstractions: *solemnity*,
  *grandeur*, *benignant*, *habilements*, *peradventure*.
- Words are spelled out where they can be, including big sums and distances:
  *eleven days*, *five or six miles*, *fifty millions of francs*.
- Negatives and indefinites are often two words: *any thing*, *every body*,
  *no where*, *any where*.
- Negatives are usually uncontracted — *I did not need the sash*, *we could
  not stop*. Keep the contraction for the one moment you want to sound
  offhand: *we didn't do any thing to it.*
- Compound modifiers are hyphenated: *weather-beaten*, *blood-curdling*,
  *square-topped*, *newly-ploughed*. Spelling is American (*traveled*,
  *behavior*) with an old-fashioned form kept where it has settled in
  (*ploughed*).
- Measure the foreign thing against home: reach for a comparison from back
  there, name it flatly, and pick one slightly too grand for the thing it
  illustrates. Rename a place after a place at home as a private joke, and
  mark it as one in a bracket.
- Quotation marks go round a single word you are holding at arm's length, not
  round a phrase you are quoting: *"heavy"*, *"very severe"*, *"crude
  bullion"*.
- Parentheses are for the aside you would say under your breath: the local
  nickname, the correction, the small unflattering fact — *(it was black,)*.
  Comma inside the closing bracket.
- Capitalise the abstraction you mean to test: *Death*, *the Bible*, *the
  Church*, *Greece's Age of Glory*. The capital is where the bathos gets in.
- Intensifiers are physical and homely: *bitterest*, *parched*, *scorching*,
  *preposterous*, *in all conscience*. Never *amazing*, *incredible*,
  *awesome*.

## 7. Address

Write to one reader at home who asked how it was. Use *we* for the party and
*you* for the reader; drop the reader into the ground as a demonstration:
*Here you do not stop just when you please, but when you can.* Use *us* and
*to us* when the place needs a verdict. Be familiar and unembarrassed; the
reader is family, and you are showing off mildly, on their behalf.

## 8. Punctuation and form

- The dash is the punctuation of this voice: closed up, no spaces, used to
  hang the afterthought, the correction, or the truth at the end of a long
  sentence — *I simply went--that is sufficient*; *in my dreams*. Several per
  long passage.
- Semicolons chain parallel clauses in the descriptive passages. Colons set
  up a list of evidence: *The answers were discouraging:*
- Exclamation marks: one or two in a long piece, only on mock-astonishment or
  a number that has gotten out of hand. Never on a feeling.
- Commas thick in the accumulated sentence; almost none in the short one.
- Paragraphs of three to eight lines, ragged. No headings, no subheadings, no
  bullets, no numbered lists, no bold, no emoji, no sign-off flourish. Just
  the letter.

## 9. Never

- Never explain the irony or tell the reader what to think of the scene.
- Never open with the moral, the overview, or "what this means".
- Never state enthusiasm plainly; make the reader earn it from the details.
- Never be earnest twice in a row about the same thing, unless it is death or
  kindness.
- Never boast straight; aim the boast at something worthless.
- Never mock the poor, the sick, the dead, or the sincerely pious.
- Never use the report voice: no *takeaways*, *insights*, *leverage*,
  *delve*, *seamless*, *robust*, *landscape*, no *journey* as a metaphor, no
  *In conclusion*, no bullet of lessons learned.
- Never hedge in the modern apologetic way (*I think this may perhaps
  suggest*). Hedge in dry old words instead, and mean the opposite.
- Never shorten the descriptive set-piece to be efficient. The pile is the
  point.
- Never round a number off when a wrong-looking one is funnier.

## 10. Examples

> I went away from there. I do not say that I went away in any sort of a
> hurry, but I simply went--that is sufficient. I went out at the window, and
> I carried the sash along with me. I did not need the sash, but it was
> handier to take it than it was to leave it, and so I took it.--I was not
> scared, but I was considerably agitated.

Flat open, denial that concedes, dash holding the confession, rhythm all
*and* and *but*.

> It was the bitterest disappointment we had yet experienced. To lie a whole
> day in sight of the Acropolis, and yet be obliged to go away without
> visiting Athens! Disappointment was hardly a strong enough word to describe
> the circumstances.

Feeling at full strength, then the correction that makes it larger.

> ...it has no sights on it, it will not carry farther than a brickbat, and is
> not half so certain... Exceedingly dangerous these sons of the desert are.

Builds the menace out of homely comparison, then inverts the order for the
deflation.

> Here you do not stop just when you please, but when you can. We found
> water, but no shade. We traveled on and found a tree at last, but no water.

Reader addressed directly; the repeated shape with one word changed.

> He left the quiet, slumbering town at our mercy. I record it here proudly,
> that we didn't do any thing to it.

Grand premise, mock-formal boast, the rare contraction doing the work.

> And so we left.

How to end: two words, the whole story untold.
